title: The mountains remain
hook: Du Fu in wartime: the nation is broken, mountains and rivers remain (Spring View, 757)
tomorrow: an empty mountain, voices, no one in sight. where's the light?

segments.voice: A week of small lines: and yet; don't swat; the comb; borrowed water; thinking of home. Yesterday's: the moon and my shadow, alone and in good company. Now a harder spring.
screen: `THE MOON AND MY SHADOW.` → `A WEEK OF SMALL LINES.`

segments.voice: Some weeks the news makes it feel like everything is breaking at once. Du Fu lived through that. A rebellion has taken the capital, and he's stuck inside the captured city, his family far away. He writes: the nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain. Spring comes to the city anyway, and the grass and trees grow deep.
screen: `EVERYTHING BREAKING AT ONCE.` → `STUCK IN THE CAPTURED CITY.` → `MOUNTAINS AND RIVERS REMAIN.`

segments.voice: The poem doesn't stay calm. Feeling the times, he says, even flowers draw tears; hating the parting, even birds startle the heart. A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold. His white hair is so thin it can barely hold a hairpin. Notice the order: he names the break first. Only then does he look for what's still standing. You've met that first line on this path already: it's the one Basho remembered, weeping, at Hiraizumi. Tradition calls Du Fu the poet-sage, and the sage he stands nearest is Confucius, who said, in Legge's English: "When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves." Hard winters show what lasts. Under the mountains sits a Confucian teaching: goodness is proved by steadiness when things fall apart, the evergreen in the cold. Du Fu doesn't pretend the nation is fine, and he doesn't pretend the hills are gone.
screen: `FLOWERS DRAW TEARS.` · `NAME THE BREAK FIRST.` · `THE PINE IN THE COLD.` · `STEADINESS PROVES GOODNESS.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAINS REMAIN.`

segments.voice: Count what remains. On your fingers, one at a time, name something still standing in your life this week: a person, a place, a habit, a body that breathes. Don't skip the hard things; let the count sit beside them.
The mountains remain: Du Fu's broken city, and the hills still standing around it.
Carry this one: the mountains remain, so name the break, then find the pine. One week of poets, done.

screen: `DAY 1547 COUNTS.` → `POET CARD: DU FU · 14 OF 21.` → `TOMORROW: AN EMPTY MOUNTAIN, VOICES, NO ONE IN SIGHT. WHERE'S THE LIGHT?`

howItsDone: Readers return to Du Fu's Spring View in hard times. Confucian teaching holds up the pine and cypress, green in winter, as the picture of steady goodness.

chat.meaning: Du Fu wrote 'the nation is broken' before 'mountains and rivers remain.' Like Confucius's pine in winter, what lasts shows up in hard times.
